item.title: The Last Lighthouse Keeper Has Four Visitors
item.hook: You inherit a remote lighthouse for one stormy month. A rescue pilot, a marine biologist, a bestselling novelist, and the island mayor each arrive with a reason to stay—and none intends to let the others win your heart.

# Story Idea

## Title
The Last Lighthouse Keeper Has Four Visitors

## Hook
You inherit a remote lighthouse for one stormy month. A rescue pilot, a marine biologist, a bestselling novelist, and the island mayor each arrive with a reason to stay—and none intends to let the others win your heart.

## Themes
Coastal romance, Forced proximity, Multiple male love interests, Cozy mystery, Emotional choice

You read it three times on the ferry crossing, the words blurring with salt spray: your great-aunt Maren has left you Thornwick Lighthouse, perched on a basalt finger of rock off the northern Scottish coast. The condition is simple—keep the light burning for one full month, and the lighthouse is yours forever.

You are thirty-two, recently redundant from a publishing house in Edinburgh, and carrying a half-finished manuscript in your suitcase that you have not shown a single soul. The lighthouse feels like a dare.

The ferry groans against the dock at Thornwick Island as October rain needles your cheeks. The village is a scatter of whitewashed cottages with slate roofs, a pub called The Salted Crow, and a general store with hand-painted signs. Beyond it, the lighthouse rises white against a pewter sky, its lamp dark for the first time in one hundred and forty years.

You climb the path with your suitcase rattling over wet cobblestones. The door is unlocked. Inside, the air smells of lamp oil and dried lavender. Maren's things remain—a wool blanket folded on the cot, a kettle on the stove, a shelf of tide charts and navigation manuals. On the desk, a leather-bound journal with her initials pressed into the cover.

You set your suitcase down. The silence is enormous.

Then you hear it—the distant thrum of a helicopter rotor, growing louder, until a red-and-white rescue chopper banks low over the lighthouse and settles on the flat headland to the north. Through the window, you watch a tall figure in a flight suit jump down, remove his helmet, and shake dark hair free of the rain.

Your phone buzzes. A text from an unknown number: *Welcome to Thornwick. I'm Callum Bryce, search-and-rescue pilot stationed here for the month. Your aunt and I were friends. If you need anything, the radio frequency is 121.5.*

Before you can reply, headlights sweep across the yard below. A battered Land Rover pulls up, and a lean man in a waxed jacket steps out, carrying a crate of equipment. He looks up at your window and waves with easy confidence.

He does not wave. He simply looks up at the lighthouse with an expression of quiet hunger, as though he has come home to a place he has only ever imagined.

The phone again: *Rowan Ashworth. Novelist. I've rented the keeper's cottage for the month. Your aunt said I'd find inspiration here. I intend to.*

"There," he shouts over the wind, pointing to a cove where the rocks form a natural breakwater. "We can shelter there if it gets bad."

"I know," you say. "But I wanted to walk."

He nods. Something moves behind his eyes—hurt, maybe, or the effort of containing it. "Right. Good night, then."

After he leaves, Finn makes you hot chocolate and sits close on the narrow couch, his knee pressed to yours. "He's a good man," Finn says quietly. "Callum. He's a good man, and he's in love with you. I need you to know I see that. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."

"Because I want you to choose me. But I want you to choose me with your eyes open. Knowing what you'd be leaving."

On the table, a note in Rowan's handwriting: *I heard you went with Finn. I hope you were safe. I hope you were brave. I'll be here when you're ready to come back to the quiet. —R.*

The island settles into a strange, crystalline calm. The sea is glass. The sky is the pale blue of a robin's egg. And the three men, as if by unspoken agreement, make their final moves.

Callum finds you on the headland at dawn, watching the sunrise paint the water gold. He stands beside you in silence for a long time. Then: "I put in for a permanent posting here. Thornwick. I turned down the mainland base." He looks at you. "I did it for me. But I won't pretend you weren't part of the reason." His hand finds yours. His grip is steady, warm, certain. "Stay with me. Not because I can protect you—you don't need that. But because I think we could build something here. Together. A life with the sky and the sea and the light."

Finn comes to you at the seal rocks, where the pups are fat and noisy and the colony is thriving. He is holding a single piece of sea glass—deep green, worn smooth. "I found this on my first day here," he says. "I've been carrying it around like a talisman. I was saving it for the right moment." He presses it into your palm and closes your fingers over it. "I'm leaving at the end of the month. The research is done. But I don't want to leave alone. Come with me. Not to follow me—to walk beside me. There are coastlines all over the world that need people who aren't afraid of the hard things."

Rowan comes last, at night, when the lamp is turning and the island is dark and quiet. He knocks on the lighthouse door and you let him in, and he stands in the kitchen with his notebook in his hands and an expression of terrified hope. "I finished the chapter," he says. "The one about you. About the woman who keeps the light." He sets the notebook on the table. "Read it. And then tell me if I've got you right. Because if I have—if I truly see you—then I want to spend the rest of my life seeing you. Not protecting you. Not saving you. Just... witnessing you. Writing you down. Being the person who knows every word you've ever spoken." His voice breaks slightly. "I know I'm not the bravest choice. I'm not the strongest or the most exciting. But I will never stop paying attention to you. I promise you that."

Three men. Three futures. The lamp turns overhead, patient and eternal.

You think of Maren's journal. *The island chooses who it sends you. Trust the choosing.*

But it is not the island who decides. It is you.

He teaches you to read the weather from the cloud formations, and you teach him to read your manuscript aloud, your voice steady for the first time.

You kiss him at three thousand feet, with the sea glittering below and the lamp still turning beneath you, faithful and bright.

meta.title: The Last Lighthouse Keeper Has Four Visitors
meta.logline: You inherit a remote lighthouse for one stormy month. A rescue pilot, a marine biologist, a bestselling novelist, and the island mayor each arrive with a reason to stay—and none intends to let the others win your heart.

factLabels.helped_finn: You helped Finn with his research

nodes.title: The Inheritance
nodes.body:
The solicitor's letter smells of pipe tobacco and old decisions. You read it three times on the ferry crossing, the words blurring with salt spray: your great-aunt Maren has left you Thornwick Lighthouse, perched on a basalt finger of rock off the northern Scottish coast. The condition is simple—keep the light burning for one full month, and the lighthouse is yours forever.

You are thirty-two, recently redundant from a publishing house in Edinburgh, and carrying a half-finished manuscript in your suitcase that you have not shown a single soul. The lighthouse feels like a dare.

The ferry groans against the dock at Thornwick Island as October rain needles your cheeks. The village is a scatter of whitewashed cottages with slate roofs, a pub called The Salted Crow, and a general store with hand-painted signs. Beyond it, the lighthouse rises white against a pewter sky, its lamp dark for the first time in one hundred and forty years.

You climb the path with your suitcase rattling over wet cobblestones. The door is unlocked. Inside, the air smells of lamp oil and dried lavender. Maren's things remain—a wool blanket folded on the cot, a kettle on the stove, a shelf of tide charts and navigation manuals. On the desk, a leather-bound journal with her initials pressed into the cover.

You set your suitcase down. The silence is enormous.

Then you hear it—the distant thrum of a helicopter rotor, growing louder, until a red-and-white rescue chopper banks low over the lighthouse and settles on the flat headland to the north. Through the window, you watch a tall figure in a flight suit jump down, remove his helmet, and shake dark hair free of the rain.

Your phone buzzes. A text from an unknown number: *Welcome to Thornwick. I'm Callum Bryce, search-and-rescue pilot stationed here for the month. Your aunt and I were friends. If you need anything, the radio frequency is 121.5.*

Before you can reply, headlights sweep across the yard below. A battered Land Rover pulls up, and a lean man in a waxed jacket steps out, carrying a crate of equipment. He looks up at your window and waves with easy confidence.

Another text: *Finn Okafor, marine biologist. I'll be studying the seal colony on the east rocks. Maren gave me permission to use the boathouse. Hope that's still alright?*

You are still processing when a third vehicle arrives—a black sedan, incongruous on the island's rough tracks. A man steps out in a dark coat, silver at his temples, carrying a leather satchel. He does not wave. He simply looks up at the lighthouse with an expression of quiet hunger, as though he has come home to a place he has only ever imagined.

The phone again: *Rowan Ashworth. Novelist. I've rented the keeper's cottage for the month. Your aunt said I'd find inspiration here. I intend to.*

Three men. One island. One month of storms.

You look at Maren's journal on the desk, then out at the darkening sky. The lamp needs lighting tonight. You have a choice to make about how you spend your first evening.

choices.text: Light the lamp immediately and weather the approaching storm alone, proving you can handle this.

nodes.title: First Light
nodes.body:
You climb the spiral stairs—one hundred and twelve steps, you count—and find the lamp room intact. The Fresnel lens is a cathedral of glass prisms, each one hand-cut. You follow Maren's notes, taped to the wall in her cramped handwriting, and coax the mechanism to life. The beam sweeps out over black water, and somewhere in the darkness, a ship's horn answers.

The storm hits at midnight. Rain hammers the tower like gravel thrown by an angry hand. You sit in the watch room with Maren's journal open on your knee, reading her entries from decades past. She writes about the sea, the birds, the loneliness—and then, in a later entry, about the people who came to fill it.

*The island chooses who it sends you,* she wrote. *Trust the choosing.*

By morning, the storm has spent itself. You descend to find the world rinsed clean and glittering. And you find visitors.

Callum Bryce is already at your door, two mugs of coffee in hand. He is tall and broad-shouldered, with the kind of weathered hands that suggest he has pulled people from wreckage. His eyes are the grey-green of the sea in shallow water. "Saw your light last night," he says. "Knew you'd managed it. Maren would be proud." He offers you a mug. His fingers brush yours, and the coffee is exactly how you take it—black, no sugar. "She told me how you liked it. Years ago, when you visited as a girl."

Before you can respond to the strangeness of being remembered so precisely, Finn Okafor appears on the path, wetsuit peeled to his waist, dark skin gleaming with salt water. He grins up at you. "The seals have pups! I counted fourteen this morning. I need to set up monitoring equipment on the east rocks—could use a second pair of hands for an hour, if you're free."

And from the direction of the keeper's cottage, Rowan Ashworth emerges with a notebook in hand, already writing as he walks. He looks up, sees the three of you gathered, and his mouth curves into a knowing smile. "Ah," he says. "The cast assembles." His accent is soft, southern English, educated. He looks at you directly. "I'd like to interview you for my book. About Maren. About what it means to keep a light burning in a world that has forgotten why."

Three invitations. Three pairs of eyes on you. The morning stretches out, golden and full of possibility.

You must choose how to spend it.

choices.text: Help Finn set up his monitoring equipment on the east rocks—his enthusiasm is infectious, and you want to see the seals.
Accept Rowan's invitation to talk about Maren—his quiet intensity intrigues you, and you want to understand why he came.

nodes.title: The Seal Rocks
nodes.body:
Finn leads you down a goat path to the island's eastern shore, where black rocks jut from churning water like the spines of buried giants. He talks constantly—not nervously, but with the genuine excitement of someone who has found a rare audience for his passion.

"Grey seals," he says, pointing to a cluster of silver shapes hauled out on the rocks. "They're declining across the North Sea. This colony is one of the last healthy ones. If I can document their breeding success this month, it could change the conservation designation for the whole archipelago." He turns to you, and his eyes are bright. "I know it sounds dry. But watching them—it's like watching a civilization. They have politics. Friendships. Grudges."

You spend the morning hauling equipment across slick rocks, anchoring cameras, and recording data while Finn narrates the seals' lives like a nature documentary. He is funny, warm, and completely unselfconscious about his own brilliance. When you slip on a wet rock, he catches your arm with a reflex speed that surprises you both. His grip is firm and sure.

"Careful," he says, and his voice drops half a register. "The rocks don't forgive." He doesn't let go immediately. You are aware of the heat of his palm through your jacket, the salt in his hair, the way he looks at you as though you are something he wants to study with the same devotion he gives the seals.

When you return to the lighthouse, Callum is waiting on the bench outside your door. He stands when he sees you, and his expression shifts—a flicker of something possessive and quickly controlled. "I flew over the east rocks this morning," he says casually. "Saw you two down there. Finn's a good man. But those rocks are dangerous in a swell." He hands you a thermos. "Soup. You look cold."

Finn, still behind you, says lightly, "She was perfectly safe with me, Callum."

Callum's smile doesn't reach his eyes. "Of course she was."

The tension between them is a living thing. You take the soup and thank Callum, and feel the weight of both their gazes as you climb the stairs to your door.

That evening, you find a note slipped under the lighthouse door in unfamiliar handwriting—Rowan's elegant script: *I saw you on the rocks today from my window. You looked like a woman discovering she is braver than she thought. I'd still like that conversation, whenever you're ready. —R.*

You sit with Maren's journal and read an entry from 1987: *Three men came to the island this autumn. The sea will decide which one stays. But I think it is not the sea who decides at all.*

The lamp needs winding. Outside, the wind is rising again.

nodes.title: The Novelist's Question
nodes.body:
Rowan's cottage is small and immaculate. He has already unpacked his books—spines lined up by colour, a ritual he explains with a self-deprecating smile. "Occupational neurosis. I can't write unless everything is ordered."

He makes tea in a brown pot and sits across from you at a table worn smooth by decades of keepers' elbows. His questions are precise and unexpected. Not *what did Maren mean to you?* but *what did she make you believe was possible?*

You find yourself telling him about your manuscript—the one you've never shown anyone. About the fear that lives in your chest like a cold stone. About coming here because you needed a place where no one knew your name or your failure.

Rowan listens with an intensity that is almost physical. When you finish, he says, "You're not a failure. You're a woman standing at the edge of something, and the vertigo is making you call it falling." He reaches across the table and covers your hand with his. His skin is dry and warm, his fingers long. "Let me read it. When you're ready. Not before."

The moment holds. Then the door opens without a knock, and Callum Bryce fills the frame, still in his flight suit, helmet under his arm. "Sorry to interrupt. I brought fuel for the generator—your aunt's setup runs on diesel, and I know the delivery isn't due for another week." His eyes move from your hand to Rowan's face, and something tightens in his jaw. "Didn't realize you had company."

"The door was open," Rowan says pleasantly. "Tea?"

"I'll leave you to it." Callum sets a canister by the door. But he doesn't go. He leans against the frame and looks at you directly. "There's a weather window tomorrow. Clear skies. I could take you up in the helicopter—show you the island from above. Maren always said the view from the air was the only way to understand this place."

It is not subtle. Rowan's eyebrows rise fractionally. "How generous of you, Callum."

"She's the keeper," Callum says simply. "She should know what she's keeping."

After Callum leaves, Rowan refills your tea and says, "He's in love with you. You realize that." It is not a question. "He loved Maren too, I think. Not romantically—like a daughter. And now he's transferred all that devotion to you." He pauses. "I don't say that to diminish it. I say it because I want you to know that what I feel is different. I don't want to protect you. I want to *know* you."

You walk back to the lighthouse in the blue dusk, your mind full. On your doorstep, a small crate: Finn has left a jar of sea glass, polished smooth, with a note: *Found these on the east beach. The green ones are rare. They reminded me of your eyes. —F.*

Three men. Three offerings. The lamp above you turns its slow circle, indifferent to the complications below.

nodes.title: The Storm Within
nodes.body:
A week passes. You settle into the rhythm of the lighthouse—winding the mechanism at dawn, checking the weather logs, walking the island's perimeter in the afternoons. The three men orbit you like planets with competing gravities.

Callum fixes things. Your door hinge, the crack in the watch room window, the loose step on the spiral stair. He appears with tools and strong hands and says little, but watches you with an attention that feels like being held. One evening, he brings you a hand-drawn map of the island's walking paths, annotated in his careful handwriting. "So you don't get lost," he says. "The fog comes in fast here."

Finn brings you into his world. He teaches you to identify seal calls, shows you how to read tide charts, and once, when a pup gets tangled in fishing line, lets you be the one to cut it free. His hands guide yours on the scissors, and afterward, he kisses your temple—quick, warm, gone before you can decide what it means. "Thank you," he says. "For not being afraid of the hard things."

Rowan brings you words. He reads to you from his notebooks—passages about Maren, about the sea, about a woman who keeps a light burning. You realize, with a start, that the woman is you. He is writing you into his book. "Is that alright?" he asks, and his vulnerability is so naked it steals your breath. "I can stop. I can burn it all."

"Don't," you whisper.

The island mayor, a brisk woman named Isla, stops by on her weekly supply run. She looks at the three men circling you and laughs. "Maren had the same problem in '87," she says. "Three men, one autumn. She chose the sea."

"What does that mean?" you ask.

"You'll see."

On the eighth night, a storm warning flashes on the radio. Callum's voice comes through, professional and calm: "All vessels seek shelter. Gale force nine expected by midnight. Lighthouse keeper, ensure lamp is secured and backup generator is fueled."

You check the generator. It's running low. The fuel depot is on the far side of the island—a twenty-minute walk in daylight, impossible in the dark with a gale approaching.

Your phone lights up with three messages, almost simultaneous.

Callum: *I can fly you to the depot and back before the storm hits. Trust me.*

Finn: *I know a shortcut along the shore. I'll walk with you. We'll make it.*

Rowan: *Stay inside. I'll go get the fuel myself. You shouldn't risk it.*

The wind is already rising. You have minutes to decide.

choices.text: Fly with Callum. He's a professional, and the helicopter is the fastest option.
choices.meaning: Trust in Callum's competence and protection

choices.text: Walk the shore path with Finn. You want to face the storm together, on the ground.
choices.meaning: Partnership and shared courage with Finn

nodes.title: Above the Storm
nodes.body:
The helicopter lifts off the headland pad with a roar that vibrates in your teeth. Callum's hands move across the controls with a surgeon's precision, and the island drops away beneath you—a dark shape ringed with white foam.

"Hold on," he says over the headset, and banks hard into the wind. The machine shudders. Rain streams sideways across the canopy. You grip the armrests and watch the sea below churn into something monstrous and beautiful.

"You're afraid," he says. Not a question.

"Terrified."

He glances at you, and his mouth twitches. "Good. Fear means you're paying attention." He reaches over and squeezes your knee—brief, grounding. "I've flown in worse. I promise I'll get you home."

The fuel depot is a corrugated shed on the island's western point. You land, fill the canisters, and lift off again with minutes to spare. The storm is a wall now, black and absolute, swallowing the horizon.

Halfway back, the wind hits. The helicopter lurches sideways. You cry out. Callum's jaw sets, his arms steady on the controls, and he fights the machine through the turbulence with a focus that is almost frightening in its intensity. When the lighthouse appears through the rain, he exhales for the first time in what feels like an hour.

He lands. Kills the engine. And then turns to you in the sudden silence and says, "I need you to know something. I didn't offer to fly you because it was the fastest option. I offered because I wanted you to see what I see. This island from above. The way the light hits the water." His voice roughens. "Maren showed me that view when I was twenty-two and broken. It saved me. I wanted it to save you too."

You stare at him. Rain runs down the canopy in silver threads. His eyes are very green.

"Callum—"

"You don't have to say anything. But I need you to know that what I feel isn't about Maren. It never was. It's about the way you stood in the lamp room that first night and didn't call for help. It's about the way you write in that notebook of yours when you think no one can see." He swallows. "I see you. That's all. I just wanted you to know."

You carry the fuel together in silence. At the lighthouse door, he presses the canister into your hands and his fingers linger. "Light the lamp," he says softly. "I'll watch from the air."

Inside, you find a note from Rowan on the kitchen table: *I went to get the fuel myself, but Callum beat me to it. I'm glad. I would have walked into that storm for you, but he flew. I can't compete with wings. I can only offer you my words, and the truth: you are the most extraordinary person I have ever met. —R.*

And from Finn, a text: *Saw the chopper go up. You're safe. That's what matters. But next time, let me walk beside you. I'm better on the ground. —F.*

The lamp turns. The storm rages. And you are loved, in three different languages, by three different men.

nodes.title: Along the Shore
nodes.body:
Finn meets you at the base of the lighthouse steps with two waterproof bags and a torch. "The shore path is exposed," he says, "but the tide's low. We have a window." His grin is reckless and bright. "Ready?"

You go. The path is a ribbon of wet stone between the cliff base and the sea, and the waves are already building, sending spray over your heads. Finn walks close beside you, his shoulder brushing yours, pointing out handholds where the path narrows.

"There," he shouts over the wind, pointing to a cove where the rocks form a natural breakwater. "We can shelter there if it gets bad."

It gets bad. The wind shifts, and suddenly the sea is coming over the path in solid sheets. Finn grabs your hand and pulls you into the cove, and you press against the rock face together, breathing hard, salt water streaming down your faces. His body is warm against yours. He looks down at you and laughs—a wild, joyful sound.

"This is insane," you say.

"Completely."

"We could die."

"Probably not." He tucks a strand of wet hair behind your ear. His hand stays on your cheek. "But if we did, I'd want to be here. With you. In the middle of something."

The moment stretches. The storm howls. His thumb traces your cheekbone. Then he steps back, professional again. "Come on. The depot's another ten minutes."

You get the fuel. You walk back. And somewhere on the return path, with the wind at your backs and the lighthouse beam sweeping overhead like a searchlight, Finn takes your hand and doesn't let go until you reach the door.

Inside, dry and shaking, you find Callum waiting. He is sitting at the kitchen table with a mug of tea he clearly made himself, and his expression when he sees your joined hands is carefully, painfully neutral.

"You're safe," he says. "That's what matters." But his voice is flat, and he stands too quickly, and at the door he pauses. "I could have flown you. You know that."

"I know," you say. "But I wanted to walk."

He nods. Something moves behind his eyes—hurt, maybe, or the effort of containing it. "Right. Good night, then."

After he leaves, Finn makes you hot chocolate and sits close on the narrow couch, his knee pressed to yours. "He's a good man," Finn says quietly. "Callum. He's a good man, and he's in love with you. I need you to know I see that. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."

"Why are you telling me this?"

"Because I want you to choose me. But I want you to choose me with your eyes open. Knowing what you'd be leaving."

On the table, a note in Rowan's handwriting: *I heard you went with Finn. I hope you were safe. I hope you were brave. I'll be here when you're ready to come back to the quiet. —R.*

The storm breaks over the island like a wave. The lamp holds. And you sit in the warm kitchen with the taste of chocolate on your lips and three men's words echoing in your chest.

nodes.title: The Choosing
nodes.body:
The storm passes. Three days remain in your month.

The island settles into a strange, crystalline calm. The sea is glass. The sky is the pale blue of a robin's egg. And the three men, as if by unspoken agreement, make their final moves.

Callum finds you on the headland at dawn, watching the sunrise paint the water gold. He stands beside you in silence for a long time. Then: "I put in for a permanent posting here. Thornwick. I turned down the mainland base." He looks at you. "I did it for me. But I won't pretend you weren't part of the reason." His hand finds yours. His grip is steady, warm, certain. "Stay with me. Not because I can protect you—you don't need that. But because I think we could build something here. Together. A life with the sky and the sea and the light."

Finn comes to you at the seal rocks, where the pups are fat and noisy and the colony is thriving. He is holding a single piece of sea glass—deep green, worn smooth. "I found this on my first day here," he says. "I've been carrying it around like a talisman. I was saving it for the right moment." He presses it into your palm and closes your fingers over it. "I'm leaving at the end of the month. The research is done. But I don't want to leave alone. Come with me. Not to follow me—to walk beside me. There are coastlines all over the world that need people who aren't afraid of the hard things."

Rowan comes last, at night, when the lamp is turning and the island is dark and quiet. He knocks on the lighthouse door and you let him in, and he stands in the kitchen with his notebook in his hands and an expression of terrified hope. "I finished the chapter," he says. "The one about you. About the woman who keeps the light." He sets the notebook on the table. "Read it. And then tell me if I've got you right. Because if I have—if I truly see you—then I want to spend the rest of my life seeing you. Not protecting you. Not saving you. Just... witnessing you. Writing you down. Being the person who knows every word you've ever spoken." His voice breaks slightly. "I know I'm not the bravest choice. I'm not the strongest or the most exciting. But I will never stop paying attention to you. I promise you that."

Three men. Three futures. The lamp turns overhead, patient and eternal.

You think of Maren's journal. *The island chooses who it sends you. Trust the choosing.*

But it is not the island who decides. It is you.

Who do you choose?

choices.text: Choose Callum. The sky, the sea, the steady hands. Build a life on the headland together.
choices.meaning: Choose safety, devotion, and the view from above

choices.text: Choose Finn. The sea glass, the wild laughter, the open horizon. Walk beside him into the unknown.
choices.meaning: Choose adventure, partnership, and the courage of the shore

choices.text: Choose Rowan. The words, the attention, the quiet fire. Be seen, completely and forever.
choices.meaning: Choose being known, witnessed, and loved in language

nodes.title: The View from Above
nodes.body:
You choose Callum.

He doesn't kiss you immediately. He looks at you for a long moment, as if making sure you're real, and then he pulls you against his chest and holds you so tightly you can feel his heartbeat through his flight suit. "Okay," he whispers into your hair. "Okay. Good."

The last three days pass in a golden blur. You light the lamp together each evening—he winds the mechanism, you trim the wick, and your hands move in tandem like a dance learned long ago. He teaches you to read the weather from the cloud formations, and you teach him to read your manuscript aloud, your voice steady for the first time.

On the final morning, he takes you up in the helicopter one last time. The island spreads below you—white lighthouse, dark rocks, the silver thread of the shore path. "This is ours now," he says. "All of it."

You kiss him at three thousand feet, with the sea glittering below and the lamp still turning beneath you, faithful and bright.

Finn leaves on the supply boat, waving from the deck with a grin that is only slightly sad. Rowan leaves his notebook on your kitchen table—the chapter about you, unfinished, with a note: *The ending is yours to write.* You keep it on the shelf beside Maren's journal.

The lighthouse is yours. The sky is yours. And Callum's hand in yours is steady as the beam that sweeps the dark water, guiding every lost thing home.

The sea opens before you, vast and silver and full of unknown shores. You lean into him and let the current carry you forward, brave and salt-stung and free.

recommendation.summary: A solitary lighthouse on a storm-battered island becomes the stage for an unforgettable month when four compelling men arrive, each with their own reason to stay—and to win your heart. Finn, a passionate marine biologist drawn to the seals; Rowan, a bestselling novelist haunted by a mysterious connection to the island; Callum, a steady rescue pilot who commands the skies; and the enigmatic island mayor all orbit your world as the weather closes in. Through branching choices—from helping set up monitoring equipment on the rocks to accepting a quiet conversation about a woman named Maren—you shape not only the romance but the mystery woven into the lighthouse's past. The story builds toward a final, deeply personal choice: the sky, the shore, or the quiet fire of being truly seen. Atmospheric, cozy, and emotionally rich, this is a love letter to slow-burn connection set against the wild beauty of the coast.
